As per the prosecution case as unfurled in the first information report lodged by one Raghunandan is that in the intervening night of 12/13.03.2012, his son Sukhdev, aged about 28 years was sleeping in his fields under the Pakar tree so as to ensure the safety of engine kept in his fields.
4.
He further alleged that on the next morning at about 7:00 AM, when he went in his fields, then he saw his son Sukhdev lying dead under the Pakar tree and was soaked with blood with numerous injuries.
5. It is further alleged that number of litigations are pending between him and the accused-respondents.

It is further alleged that Mahesh, Ghulam Nabi and his another son Rajesh had also over heard them conversing against him and a suspicion was raised that the accused-respondents had infact killed his son Sukhdev, while he was asleep.

6. On the basis of a written report, a first information report was lodged at Police Station Bunda,
District Shahjahanpur vide Case Crime No. 56 of 2012, under Section 302 IPC.
7.

After registration of the first information report, the investigation of the said case was entrusted to PW-6 Ravindra Pratap Singh, who recorded the statement of the first informant Raghunandan and thereafter, reached the place of incident and prepared the site plan.

The Investigating Officer thereafter collected the blood-stained earth and plain earth from the place of incident and had also collected the sample of blood-stained mattress form the place of incident.

8. Thereafter, Investigating Officer had instructed S.I. Sahbul Hasan to conduct the inquest on the person of the deceased, who prepared the inquest memo and after preparing the relevant documents, wrapped the dead body in a plain cloth and handed it over to the Constable for carrying it to the Mortuary for the post-mortem.

An autopsy was conducted on the person of the deceased on 12.02.2012 at 4:50 PM and the Doctor has found four stabbed wound injuries on the person of the deceased and has noted that the cause of death is shock and haemorrhage as a result of anti-mortem injuries.
9.

Subsequently on 16.03.2012, on the information given by the informer, accused-respondents Mahipal and Rampal were arrested and their confessional statements were also recorded and thereafter, accused-respondent Rampal got recovered a spear from under the culvert, which was taken in possession by the Investigating Officer, who prepared the fard recovery memo, which has been proved and marked as Exhibit Ka-10.
10.

The Investigating Officer thereafter recorded the statement of the relevant witnesses and after concluding the investigation, submitted the charge-sheet against the accused-respondents Mahipal and Rampal, however, charge-sheet was submitted against accused-respondent Sushil as an absconder.
11.

Since the case was exclusively triable by the court of Sessions, it was committed to the court of Sessions for trial, where it was registered vide Sessions Trial No. 376 of 2014 (State of U.P. Vs.

sentences.text: After committal of the case, learned Trial Court framed the charges against the accused-respondents under Sections 302 IPC.
The said charges were read out and explained to the accused-respondents, who abjured the charges, pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried.

13. The prosecution in order to prove the guilt against the accused-respondents has produced PW-1 Raghunandan, being the first informant, PW-2 Nanhe Lal, real brother of the deceased, Panch witness and witness of recovery of blood-stained earth and blood soaked mattress, PW-3 Mahesh and PW-4 Ghulam Nabi, who are alleged to have seen the accused-respondents coming from the place of incident after the murder, PW-5 Rajesh, another son of the first informant Raghunandan,
who have stated that two days prior to the incident, he had over heard the accused-respondents conversing amongst them to cause harm to his family and had further stated that PW-3 Mahesh and PW-4 Ghulam Nabi had informed him that the accused-respondents killed his brother while he was sleeping.
14.
After recording the testimony of the prosecution witnesses, the statements of the accused-respondents under Section 313 CrPC were recorded, wherein they have denied the prosecution story.

The accused-respondent Rampal has stated that he is an innocent and prior to the incident, he had lodged a criminal case under SC/ST Act against PW-1 Raghunandan and his son,
consequent to which, they were sent to jail and on account of this enmity, he has been falsely implicated.
15.

Similarly, accused-respondent Mahipal has stated that he is wholly innocent and since had assisted Rampal in lodging a criminal case under SC/ST Act against the first informant Raghunandan, consequent to which, he used to bear enmity with him and has thus falsely implicated him.

16. The accused-respondent Sushil stated that he is wholly innocent and had lodged a criminal case under the IPC against the first informant's family, in which, they have remained in jail for 4-5 months.

He further stated that there was some money due from the first informant and on asking to return the same, he was attacked upon and on account of this enmity, he has been falsely implicated,
however, none of the three accused-respondents had led any defence evidence, either oral or documentary.
17.

After recording the entire testimony of the relevant witnesses and hearing the accused-respondents, the Trial Court acquitted all the three accused-respondents of the offence under Section 302 IPC vide impugned judgment and order dated 24.03.2018.

18. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied by the said judgment and order, the instant government appeal has been preferred by the State of U.P. alongwith an application for grant of leave to appeal with the prayer to reverse the finding of acquittal recorded by the Trial Court in favour of the accused-respondents and to convict them for the offence charged with.

Learned AGA for the State/appellant has submitted that the Trial Court has not appreciated the evidence and material on record in right perspective and has illegally recorded the finding of acquittal in favour of the accused-respondents.

20. Learned AGA for the State/ appellant has further submitted that finding of acquittal recorded by the Trial Court in favour of the accused-respondents is based on surmises and conjectures and is therefore liable to be set aside.

21. Per contra, learned counsel for the accused-respondents has submitted that in the instant case,
there is no eye-witness account of the incident and the case is squarely based on circumstantial evidence.

22. Learned counsel for the accused-respondents has further submitted that PW-1 Raghunandan is the father of the deceased, whereas PW-2 Nanhe Lal and PW-5 Rajesh are real brothers of the deceased and they have not actually witnessed the incident and they, in their testimony, had only stated that they have been informed by PW-3 Mahesh and PW-4 Ghulan Nabi to have seen the accused-respondents coming from the place of incident in a running posture just after the incident.

However, during the course of trial, neither PW-3 Mahesh nor PW-4 Ghulam Nabi have supported the prosecution story at all and have been declared hostile and thus, there is no cogent and reliable evidence to corroborate the prosecution story and the circumstances leading to the murder of the deceased.

23. Learned counsel for the accused-respondents has further submitted that though the case is based on circumstantial evidence but there is no link evidence available on record to show that the chain of circumstance is complete.

24. Learned counsel for the accused-respondents has further submitted that the prosecution case is that PW-3 Mahesh and PW-4 Ghulam Nabi had seen the accused-respondents coming from the place of incident after the murder of the deceased Sukhdev, however, during the course of trial,
neither PW-3 Mahesh nor PW-4 Ghulam Nabi has supported the prosecution story at all and have been declared hostile.

On their attention been drawn to their statement shown to be recorded under Section 161 CrPC, both of them categorically stated that they had not given any such statement to the police and they could not state as to how the Investigating Officer has recorded their such statement.
It is further germane to state that except the testimony of PW-3 Mahesh and PW-4 Ghulam Nabi, there is absolutely no evidence to connect the accused-respondents with the instant case.

25. Learned counsel for the accused-respondents has further submitted that the Trial Court after discussing the entire evidence and material on record has reached a just and fair conclusion acquitting the accused-respondents by holding that the prosecution has miserably failed to prove the case beyond all reasonable doubts against the accused-respondents, which order does not suffer from any illegality or perversity and therefore, cannot be reversed.

sentences.text: Learned counsel for the accused-respondents has further submitted that against the impugned judgment and order dated 24.03.2018, the first informant Raghunandan had preferred a criminal appeal under Section 372 CrPC alongwith an application for grant of leave to appeal.

The said application alongwith appeal was heard by co-ordinate Bench of this Court and after hearing the parties, the application for leave to appeal was rejected on merits and consequently, the appeal filed by the first informant was also dismissed vide judgment and order dated 25.05.2018.
The said order passed by the co-ordinate Bench of this Court has not been challenged before the higher court and as such, has become final.

27. Thus, in the backdrop of the said circumstances, when an appeal filed by the first informant has already been dismissed, then no leave to appeal can be granted in the instant government appeal and the same is also liable to be dismissed.

28. Having considered the rival submissions made by learned counsel for the parties and upon going through the entire evidence recorded during the course of trial, we find that the instant case is based on circumstantial evidence as there is no direct evidence to corroborate the prosecution story.
29. Admittedly, there is no direct evidence recorded during the course of trial indicating the involvement of the accused-respondents in the crime, in question.

The only evidence was in the form of testimony of PW-3 Mahesh and PW-4 Ghulam Nabi, who were alleged to have seen all the three accused-respondents coming from the place of incident, where the murder had taken place.
However, during the course of trial, both PW-3 and PW-4 have turned hostile and have not supported the prosecution story at all.

Even during the course of cross-examination, on their attention being drawn to their statement shown to be recorded under Section 161 CrPC, they have categorically stated that they have not given any such statement to the Investigating Officer and cannot state as to how the Investigating Officer has recorded their such statement.
Thus, we find that in the entire testimony, there is no link evidence to connect the accused-respondents in the instant case.

30. As far as the testimony of PW-1 Raghunandan, PW-2 Nanhe Lal and PW-5 Rajesh is concerned,
their testimony is based on hearsay.

They in their testimony have categorically stated that PW-3 Mahesh and PW-4 Ghulam Nabi had informed them to have seen the accused-respondents coming from the place of incident, however subsequently, they have resiled from their earlier version and had been declared hostile by the prosecution.
Thus, the testimony of PW-1 Raghunandan, PW-2 Nanhe Lal and PW-5 Rajesh also do not lend any credence to the prosecution story.

In the backdrop of which, the Trial Court has rightly recorded the finding of acquittal in favour of the accused-respondents, which is based on sound and cogent reasons and therefore, cannot be reversed.

31. The Hon'ble Apex Court in catena of decisions has held that in a case based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances taken cumulatively, should form a chain so complete that there is no escape from the conclusion that within all human probability the crime was committed by the accused and none else and the circumstantial evidence in order to sustain conviction must be complete and incapable of explanation of any other hypothesis than that of the guilt of the accused State Of U.P. vs Sushil And 2 Ors. on 12 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/132783996/
5 and such evidence should not only be consistent with the guilt of the accused but should be inconsistent with his innocence.

The other evidence that emerges from the fact of the present case is the recovery of a weapon at the pointing out of the co-accused-respondent Rampal, however, when we go through the evidence adduced by the prosecution to prove the said recovery, we find that the prosecution has miserably failed to prove the said recovery also.

36. Now, coming to the scope of reversal of acquittal in Government Appeal, we may say that the Hon'ble Apex Court in several of its decisions has laid down the principles governing the scope of interference by the High Court in an appeal filed by that State for challenging the acquittal of the accused recorded by the trial court.

37. This Court in the case of Rajesh Prasad Vs. State of Bihar and Another reported in (2022) 3 SCC 471 encapsulated the legal position covering the field after considering various earlier judgments and held as below:-

sentences.text: After referring to a catena of judgments, this Court culled out the following general principles regarding the powers of the appellate court while dealing with an appeal against an order of acquittal in the following words: [Chandrappa Vs. State of Karnataka, (2007) 4 SCC 415] "42.

entities.text: Chandrappa Vs. State of Karnataka, (2007) 4 SCC 415
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
From the above decisions, in our considered view,
the following general principles regarding powers of the appellate court while dealing with an appeal against an order of acquittal emerge (i) An appellate court has full power to review, re-appreciate and reconsider the evidence upon which the order of acquittal is founded.
(ii) The Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 puts no limitation, restriction or condition on exercise of such power and an appellate court on the evidence before it may reach its own conclusion, both on questions of fact and of law.
(iii) Various expressions, such as, "substantial and compelling reasons", "good and sufficient grounds", "very strong circumstances", "distorted conclusions", "glaring mistakes", etc. are not intended to curtail extensive powers of an appellate court in an appeal against acquittal.

Such phraseologies are more in the nature of "flourishes of language" to emphasise the reluctance of an appellate court to interfere with acquittal than to curtail the power of the court to review the evidence and to come to its own conclusion.
(iv) An appellate court, however, must bear in mind that in case of acquittal, there is double presumption in favour of the accused.

Firstly, the presumption of innocence is available to him under the fundamental principle of criminal jurisprudence that every person shall be presumed to be innocent unless he is proved guilty by a competent court of law.
Secondly, the accused having secured his acquittal, the presumption of his innocence is further reinforced, reaffirmed and strengthened by the trial court.

(v) If two reasonable conclusions are possible on the basis of the evidence on record,
the appellate court should not disturb the finding of acquittal recorded by the trial court."
38.

entities.text: H.D. Sundara & Ors. Vs. State of Karnataka reported in (2023) 9 SCC 581

sentences.text:
The appellate court, while deciding an appeal against acquittal, after re-appreciating the evidence, is required to consider whether the view taken by the trial court is a possible view which could have been taken on the basis of the evidence on record;
(8.4).

If the view taken is a possible view, the appellate court cannot overturn the order of acquittal on the ground that another view was also possible; and (8.5). The appellate court can interfere with the order of acquittal only if it comes to a finding that the only conclusion which can be recorded on the basis of the evidence on record was that the guilt of the accused was proved beyond a reasonable doubt and no other conclusion was possible."
39.

The appellate Court, in order to interfere with the judgment of acquittal would have to record pertinent findings on the above factors if it is inclined to reverse the judgment of acquittal rendered by the trial Court.

41. In the light of above settled proposition of law when we go through the impugned judgment and order, we find that the trial court had given cogent and convincing reasons for recording the finding of acquittal against the accused-respondents and that the acquittal of the accused-respondents is plausible and justifiable view emanating from the discussion of the evidence available on record and does not suffer from any infirmity or perversity.

42. In the backdrop of the said facts and circumstances, we are of the opinion that the impugned judgment and order passed by the trial court is just, proper and legal and do not call for any interference by this Court.
43. In view of the above, the application for grant of leave to appeal in the instant case is wholly misconceived and is liable to be outrightly rejected.
Accordingly, the prayer for grant of leave to appeal is refused and the application is rejected.

Consequently, the instant government appeal,
being devoid of merits, is also dismissed.
